summary: Someone close to you runs: {close tie} has filed for office and asks what part you will play in the campaign.
realLife: One life: In 1972 she ran her friend Sarah Weddington's winning campaign for the Texas House and worked as her aide; she had volunteered for years while raising four children. Another: At 94 she entered a U.S. Senate race days before the filing deadline after the frontrunner left the race, took only small donations and lost to the incumbent.
weights: Organizing traits and campaign work on your record.
{close tie}'s health, when they are older.
choices: help a few nights a week
keep the house running and stay out of the campaign
tell them it is a mistake, or ask why now

branches.then: The talk is who covers the evenings and the money at home. Offering to be treasurer means you sign the reports, and a mistake on them is your record.
Their health and your time are the stakes. If they lose by a lot and are proud of it, election night plays from the manager's side.
They offer you a staff job, or you stand beside them on the stage and hear their promise with everyone else.
They want a donation you think will hurt. Overruling them or giving in goes on both your records.
If the party asked you first and you declined, it comes up again on election night.
